title: 2.1.1 Training data
text: 2.1.1 Training dataIn this stage, the model does not directly process high-dimensional gene expression data. Instead, it takes the perturbation condition cond as input, which is composed of the drug molecule (SMILES), the target cell type (cell), and the drug dosage (dose). Given Nchem drugs, Ncell cell types, and Ndose dosages, the total number of unique perturbation combinations is Ncond=Nchem×Ncell×Ndose. We pre-calculate the Rsim2 ∈RNcond between the mean expression of the control group and the mean expression of the perturbed group for each condition (details are provided in Section 3, available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online). The dataset is thus defined as (cond,Rsim2). Notably, Rsim2 is used to determine whether a perturbation condition requires flow-based generation, whereas evaluation R2 measures the agreement between model-generated expression profiles and the observed perturbed profiles in Stage 2.

title: 2.1.4 Imbalance training
text: 2.1.4 Imbalance trainingTo determine the optimal strategy for mitigating the severe data imbalance in the dataset, we evaluated several established techniques, including Oversampling, Balanced MSE, and GAILoss. Specifically, the Oversampling strategy operates at the data level by selectively duplicating minority-class instances—namely, those exhibiting low Rsim2 values, which correspond to strong biological responses, to construct more balanced training batches. Alternatively, balanced MSE addresses imbalanced regression from a probabilistic perspective, modifying the standard mean squared error into a statistically principled, weighted loss function that accommodates skewed target distributions. GAI serves as an advanced refinement of this concept; it incorporates Gaussian priors to smooth the target label space, thereby reducing generalization errors in sparse, high-response regions.Our empirical evaluations demonstrate that GAI consistently achieves superior performance compared to the other baseline strategies. Consequently, we integrate the GAI-based loss into our framework. First, GAI parameterizes the empirical training distribution ptrain(Rsim2) using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM): (2) ptrain(Rsim2)=∑k=1KπkN(Rsim2;μk,Σk) where K is the number of Gaussian components, and πk,μk,Σk represent the mixture weight, mean, and covariance matrix of the k-th component, respectively.By substituting the GMM into the Balanced MSE objective, the product of two Gaussian distributions yields an unnormalized Gaussian, enabling a strictly analytical closed-form solution. Thus, the final GAI Loss function optimized in our first stage is formulated as: (3) LGAI(Rsim2,R2¯sim)=(Rsim2−R2¯sim)22σnoise2 +log ∑k=1KπkN(R2¯sim;μk,Σk+σnoise2). where σnoise2 is a learnable parameter representing the noise variance.

title: 2.2.1 Training data
text: 2.2.1 Training dataFor the generative stage, we exclusively retain perturbed gene expression samples where Rsim2 <threshold, denoted as xp∈RNgene.

title: 2.2.3 Flow matching model
text: 2.2.3 Flow matching modelWhile conventional approaches typically utilize pre-perturbation samples from the same cell type as the initial state, our empirical observations during training suggest that the marginal differences between pre- and post-perturbation profiles result in excessively slow model convergence. To address this, we instead employ a standard Gaussian distribution x0∈RNgene as the initial state for the generation process. The model defines a path between x0 and the target distribution (perturbed expression xp) by learning a time-dependent velocity field vt over the interval t∈[0,1].We use hctrl to modulate the velocity prediction via AdaLN. The control vector hctrl is projected through a linear layer and split into four modulation parameters: scaling and gating factors for the Multi-Head Self-Attention block (smsa,gmsa) and the Feed-Forward Network (smlp,gmlp): (5) smsa,gmsa,smlp,gmlp=Split(Linear(hctrl)) To improve training stability by ensuring the model behaves as an identity mapping upon initialization, we apply the following transformations: (6) g¯msa=tanh(gmsa), g¯mlp=tanh(gmlp) (7) s¯msa=1+smsa, s¯mlp=1+smlp Let MSA(·) represent the block of Multi-Head Self-Attention, FFN(·) represent Feed-Forward Network, and LN(·) represent Layer Norm block. The computation within each block is defined as follows: (8) zt=ExpEmbedder(xt) (9) ht=zt+g¯msa·LN(MSA(LN(zt)⊙s¯msa)) (10) h¯t=ht+g¯mlp·LN(FFN(LN(ht)⊙s¯mlp)) where zt∈RNgene×d is the hidden state at time t, and ExpEmbedder(·) independently projects each scalar gene-expression value xt,g into a d-dimensional gene token. Finally, the hidden state h¯t∈RNgene×d is projected back to the gene expression dimension to predict the velocity vt∈RNgene: (11) vt=Linear(h¯t) The sample at the next time step is updated as xt+1=xt+vt. The final predicted expression x¯p is obtained through multi-step ODE integration from t=0 to t=1, optimized using the MSE loss.

title: 2.2.4 Datasets and preprocessing
text: 2.2.4 Datasets and preprocessingThe single-drug perturbation datasets include SciPlex3 and McFarland. SciPlex3 contains 9-drug OOD split and two dosage splits, while McFarland includes five drug splits and three cell-type splits. The combinatorial drug perturbation dataset, ComboSciPlex, is a scRNA-seq subset derived from the combinatorial perturbation experiments in SciPlex3 and includes one drug combination split. More details are provided in Section 1, available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online.Gene expression values were normalized using log(x+1) and library size normali zation. We select the top 2000 Highly Variable Genes (HVGs) for SciPlex3 and McFarland dataset, and 1000 for ComboSciPlex dataset.For each condition, we selected the top 50 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) as a subset for additional testing (detailed selection methods are provided in Sections 1 and 2, available as supplementary data at Bioinformatics online).
